title: Georgia holds emergency meeting on AI exposing voters’ secret ballots
key_facts: Max Springer, a postdoctoral fellow at Princeton's Center for Information Technology Policy, used a $20 AI subscription and data from an Open Records Act request to test whether Georgia voters could be matched to their ballots.
He says he recovered the voting order for 1.52 million ballots, 98.9% of in-person ballots in 114 of the 139 counties he examined; in some counties he says ballot secrecy is entirely lost.
The flaw is that each scanned ballot record carries an ID that is not random enough, so its order can be matched with check-in lists or other data such as camera images.
Georgia's state elections board held an emergency meeting on Thursday 1 Oct 2026, less than two weeks before early voting starts in the midterm election.
Outgoing secretary of state Brad Raffensperger ordered ballot ID numbers redacted from public releases after an election, which cryptographer Ben Adida said 'substantially address[es] this flaw'.

Board member Salleigh Grubbs proposed having poll workers shuffle paper ballots in a tray and said redaction breaks the transparency law; county officials and board member Janelle King dismissed her proposal as problematic. The article reports no decision.
quote_evidence: Within a couple of hours, I had a pipeline to analyze and identify secret ballots across the state of Georgia and the agent told me exactly what further information it would need to identify real voters’ ballots,”

Georgia’s state elections board held an emergency meeting on Thursday morning to discuss how artificial intelligence has made it easier to identify voters through their ballot code, leaving people more vulnerable.
With early voting around the corner, changes to processes now are “a day late and about $30m short,” Sinners added.
why_it_matters_hint: AI made it cheap to link voters to ballots in Georgia just before early voting, and officials disagree on a fix.
event_date: Emergency meeting on Thursday 1 Oct 2026; Springer's test 'last month' (Sep 2026)
notes: The 98.9% and 1.52 million figures are Springer's own claims as reported by The Guardian. Linking a ballot to a named voter needs other data (check-in order, camera images). Flaw first noticed by researchers about four years ago, per the article.
